record.paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
record.original_question: For fully decentralized learning with peer-to-peer client communication, can deep-learning and stochastic-gradient-descent schemes remain robust when clients temporarily disappear, join, drop out, or experience message loss, while still converging in realistic networks?

evidence.quote: for the case of deep learning and SGD this remains an open question

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a fully decentralized learning setting in which a set of clients communicates over a peer-to-peer network (no central server). Each client $i$ holds a local data distribution $\mathcal{D}_i$ and the goal is to collaboratively train a (possibly non-convex) deep neural network model with parameters $\theta\in\mathbb{R}^d$ that approximately minimizes $F(\theta)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_i}[\ell(\theta;x)]$, by means of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) updates combined with gossip-style exchanges of parameters or gradients with neighbors in a (possibly time-varying) communication graph $G_t=(V_t,E_t)$.

Assume realistic network conditions in which:
(a) clients may temporarily disappear and later rejoin the network,
(b) new clients may join at arbitrary times,
(c) clients may permanently drop out, and
(d) messages between neighbors may be lost or delayed.

Design a decentralized SGD scheme for training deep models in this setting, and prove that it is robust to the above failure modes while still converging (in expectation, or almost surely) to a stationary point — or, more strongly, to a consensus minimizer — of $F$ under verifiable assumptions on the graph dynamics, message-loss process, step sizes, and stochastic gradient noise. Equivalently, determine whether such a robust, provably convergent decentralized SGD scheme for deep learning exists in fully decentralized peer-to-peer networks subject to client churn and message loss.
artifact.status_search_result: Recent works (2023–2025) propose partial solutions—e.g., DeceFL with O(1/T) convergence under time-invariant connected topologies, gradient-tracking schemes with local updates, dropout-resilient aggregation methods, and asynchronous decentralized FL frameworks like DRACO—but each requires restrictive assumptions (connected/time-invariant graphs, specific dropout models, convexity, or limited heterogeneity). A general provably-convergent robust decentralized SGD scheme for deep (non-convex) models under simultaneous client churn, joins, drops, and message loss in realistic peer-to-peer networks remains open.

status_evidence.title: Mitigating Persistent Client Dropout in Asynchronous Decentralized Federated Learning
status_evidence.snippet: Asynchronicity and decentralization obfuscate information about model updates among federation peers, making recovery from a client dropout difficult.
status_evidence.claim: Persistent client dropout in decentralized FL is still an active research problem with only partial mitigations.

status_evidence.title: DeceFL: a principled fully decentralized federated learning framework
status_evidence.snippet: DeceFL ... achieves the same convergence rate O(1/T) as centralized FL ... under time-invariant connected communication topologies.
status_evidence.claim: Convergence guarantees in decentralized FL exist only under restrictive (time-invariant, connected) topology assumptions.

status_evidence.title: Robust Decentralized Learning with Local Updates and Gradient Tracking
status_evidence.snippet: Gradient tracking with local updates for robust decentralized learning.
status_evidence.claim: Recent partial progress addresses heterogeneity and local updates, not full client churn plus message loss for deep models.

status_evidence.title: Privacy-Preserving, Dropout-Resilient Aggregation in Decentralized Learning
status_evidence.claim: Dropout resilience addressed only for specific aggregation/privacy settings.
